title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet
web_title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet
book_title: Chapter 6: Following the Cash — Financials & Earnings Quality
question: Are Creative Newtech's profits turning into cash, and was the swing from −₹272 Cr of operating cash flow in FY26 to +₹351 Cr in H1 FY27 genuine compounding, timing, or financing optics?

epigraph.quote: Profit is an opinion; cash is a fact.
epigraph.author: Well-known analyst's maxim

web_blocks.text: The central forensic question is a ₹623 Cr swing in operating cash flow from one period to the next. In FY26 the audited consolidated operating cash flow was −₹271.88 Cr against profit after tax of ₹70.29 Cr, and borrowings rose from ₹72 Cr to ₹324 Cr. In H1 FY27 reviewed operating cash flow was +₹351.24 Cr against profit of ₹39.47 Cr. Borrowings fell to ₹194 Cr, and the Screener ledger shows other liabilities jumping from ₹249 Cr to ₹731 Cr and total assets from ₹937 Cr to ₹1,325 Cr. [30][31][29] The H1 FY27 balance sheet, cash-flow statement and transcript let us say what drove it. One reconciliation point comes first. The Q2 FY27 deck prints FY26 operating cash flow as ₹271.88 Cr on one page and ₹273.10 Cr on another. The audited cash-flow statement says ₹27,188.34 lakh, so we use ₹271.88 Cr. [33][30]

web_blocks.title: Profit and loss: fast growth, thin and improving margins

web_blocks.caption: Consolidated profit and loss, FY19 to FY26 and trailing twelve months (Screener ledger, ₹ Cr; TTM per Screener)
web_blocks.takeaway: Sales grew from ₹368 Cr in FY19 to ₹2,704 Cr in FY26 and ₹2,883 Cr on a trailing basis. Operating margin moved from 2.8% to 3.4% and 4.1% TTM. Interest went from ₹5 Cr to ₹21 Cr and ₹30 Cr TTM, and net profit from ₹6 Cr to ₹70 Cr and ₹81 Cr, while the tax rate fell from 29% to 14%. [29]

web_blocks.text: Revenue compounded at 33% a year over FY19 to FY26, but with a stall in FY25 (+4%) and a sharp reversal inside it (Q1 FY25 −36% YoY). [29] The margin story is more modest. EBITDA before other income was 3.4% of sales in FY26 against 2.8% in FY19, so almost all of the profit growth is volume. Two things help the profit line that are not operating. The tax rate halved because profits sit increasingly in Hong Kong, and FY24 profit included a one-off ₹9.9 Cr gain on the sale of Ckart, about ₹7.7 Cr after tax. [29][37][36] On the other side of the ledger, certification, tooling and design costs are expensed rather than capitalised, which makes reported EBITDA conservative. [35]

web_blocks.caption: Nine-quarter trend, consolidated (₹ Cr; revenue, EBITDA including other income and PAT per company decks; interest per ledger, rounded except where the company prints it)
web_blocks.takeaway: Revenue growth peaked at +84% in Q4 FY26 and has slowed to +15% in Q2 FY27. EBITDA margin rose to 5.3%, and interest per quarter tripled from about ₹3 Cr to ₹9.3 Cr. [33][29][31]

web_blocks.caption: Half-year view with operating cash flow (consolidated, ₹ Cr; half-year sums of quarterly deck figures; cash flow per company decks and audited statements)
web_blocks.takeaway: Cash flow has swung by more than ₹500 Cr in a half-year in both directions. Profit moved in a ₹22 Cr to ₹41 Cr band, so profit is the stable series and working capital is the volatile one. [33][30][31]

web_blocks.title: Margin bridge: gross margin, EBITDA, interest and PAT

web_blocks.caption: Margin bridge, consolidated, as % of total income (our computation from the statements; H1 FY26 against H1 FY27 shows where the gross-margin gain went)
rows: Gross margin (total income less purchases net of stock change)
web_blocks.takeaway: Take each 100 bps of extra gross margin in H1 FY27. About 56 went to operating costs, 22 to interest, 1 to depreciation and 6 to tax, leaving only 15 bps as extra profit after tax. [30][31]

web_blocks.text: Gross margin rose 300 bps and PAT margin 44 bps, so the company is converting about 15 paise of each extra rupee of gross margin into profit. Operating costs grew faster than revenue (employee cost +73% to ₹15.99 Cr, other expenses +54% to ₹62.80 Cr). WOZOYO advertising, new country teams and the Make-in-India build are being expensed up front. Management confirms this: about ₹12 Cr of brand spend so far against a ₹20 Cr to ₹22 Cr budget, and Amazon advertising near 50% of WOZOYO sales. [31][32] Interest more than doubled to ₹16.92 Cr in H1 FY27 even though period-end debt fell, which matters for the forensic question below. [31]

web_blocks.title: Balance sheet, debt and lease forensics

web_blocks.caption: Consolidated balance sheet, March 2019 to September 2026 (Screener ledger, ₹ Cr)
web_blocks.takeaway: Borrowings rose from ₹72 Cr at March 2025 to ₹324 Cr at March 2026 and fell to ₹194 Cr at September 2026. Other liabilities went from ₹166 Cr to ₹249 Cr to ₹731 Cr, and total assets from ₹532 Cr to ₹937 Cr to ₹1,325 Cr. Reserves added only ₹37 Cr in the last six months, to ₹386 Cr. [29]

web_blocks.text: The debt is almost all short-term working-capital funding. At March 2026, ₹324.25 Cr of the ₹324.26 Cr was current. It was secured on stocks and book debts, flats and offices of promoters and a related party's gala, and guaranteed personally by Ketan and Purvi Patel. The rate was 9% to 11%, and unsecured director loans of ₹0.08 Cr carry 12%. [30] Management says ₹171 Cr of it was supply-chain finance for MSME vendors, which sits in borrowings. Crisil rated fund-based limits of ₹150.5 Cr, so about ₹174 Cr of the March borrowing sat outside the rated lines, consistent with the ₹171 Cr of vendor finance. [34][39] By September 2026 current borrowings were ₹169.40 Cr and a new non-current tranche of ₹24.60 Cr had appeared. [31] There are no lease liabilities on the balance sheet, and rent is expensed at ₹3.27 Cr. The royalty expense line, which we take to be the Honeywell licence charge, was only ₹5.96 Cr, 1.6% of Honeywell revenue. Neither leases nor royalty hide leverage. [30]

web_blocks.takeaway: In six months trade payables rose ₹282 Cr and customer advances ₹197 Cr, together ₹479 Cr. Receivables, inventory and supplier advances absorbed ₹177 Cr. The net ₹302 Cr swing took the group from ₹302 Cr of net debt to ₹30 Cr of net cash. [30][31][33]

web_blocks.title: Cash flow: what drove the swing

web_blocks.caption: Consolidated cash flow, FY19 to FY26 (Screener ledger, ₹ Cr; free cash flow is operating cash flow less capital expenditure)
web_blocks.takeaway: Operating cash flow was −₹272 Cr in FY26 against +₹22 Cr in FY25. Free cash flow was −₹275 Cr, financing inflow ₹234 Cr, and CFO ÷ operating profit −287%. Operating cash flow was negative in seven of the eight years. [29]

web_blocks.caption: Working-capital bridge from profit to operating cash flow, consolidated (₹ Cr; FY26 audited cash-flow statement, H1 FY27 reviewed cash-flow statement)
rows: The cash earned by the trading margin itself
FY26 stretched customers; H1 FY27 grew with sales but did not stretch

Advance payments to vendors, which the deck says arise because vendor credit is limited
FY26 stock-up ahead of price rises; H1 FY27 stock nearly flat
Trade payables, other financial and current liabilities (net)
The H1 FY27 inflow: suppliers and customers funded the book
Working capital: −361.90 in FY26, +293.71 in H1 FY27
web_blocks.takeaway: Of H1 FY27's ₹351.24 Cr operating cash flow, only ₹57.52 Cr came from earnings after tax. Another ₹293.71 Cr, or 84%, came from liabilities growing faster than assets. [30][31]

web_blocks.text: What drove the FY26 outflow. Of the ₹435.07 Cr put into current assets, receivables took ₹327.34 Cr (75%), inventories ₹66.09 Cr (15%) and supplier advances and other assets ₹41.64 Cr (10%). [30] Receivables rose 138% on 51% revenue growth because the revenue mix flipped. India sales jumped 165% to ₹1,797 Cr while sales outside India fell 18% to ₹903 Cr, and domestic invoices carry GST and 60 to 65 days of credit. [30][35] Debtor days went from 49 to 76 on the ledger, or from about 46 to 68 once GST on domestic sales is added to the denominator. [29][30] Had debtor days stayed at FY25's 49, FY26 operating cash flow would have been about −₹67 Cr, not −₹272 Cr. About ₹205 Cr of the outflow was therefore the stretch itself. Collectability looks sound: 96.7% of receivables were under six months old, ₹6.98 Cr (1.2%) was over a year old, and the provision was ₹0.77 Cr. [30] Management's explanation is that ‘we have to extend the extended credit’ to enter AI, surveillance and data-centre lines. It adds that days should ‘fall back to the original number’. [34]

What drove the H1 FY27 inflow. The cash-flow statement and balance sheet isolate five candidates. Trade payables rose ₹281.90 Cr to ₹467.01 Cr, from about 26 days of purchases to 66 to 77. The CFO says ‘our vendor payables days are getting extended’ and the terms were ‘negotiated very hard’. [31][32] Other current liabilities rose ₹196.82 Cr to ₹215.90 Cr. At March 2026 that line was 97% customer advances (₹185.63 Cr of ₹190.81 Cr). Advances are therefore the most likely component, and the BharatNet award is the natural source, but the September breakdown is not disclosed. [30][31] Supplier credit and buyers' credit are not separately disclosed, and TReDS financing is classified as borrowing. The ₹130 Cr fall in gross borrowings may therefore include ₹171 Cr of March TReDS balances that were repaid or re-presented as payables, but the statements do not say. [34][31] Bill discounting and factoring are not mentioned in the filings and we cannot confirm either. The fifth candidate is plain timing. Diwali fell in October last year and falls later this year, and the CMD said the quarter then under way would be the biggest. Stock purchases and receipts around it shift between quarters. [32]

The strongest clue is interest. Q2 FY27 interest of ₹9.30 Cr is the highest ever. At a 9% to 11% blended cost it implies average gross debt of about ₹340 Cr to ₹410 Cr during the quarter, against period-end debt of ₹194 Cr. [31] So the debt fell late, and the payables and advances that repaid it arrived late. That is a quarter-end snapshot, not a quarter-long average. The same pattern shows in cash: ₹206 Cr of cash at 30 September against ₹5 Cr at 31 March and ₹1.9 Cr at 30 September 2025. [31] The segment note adds that market-entry segment liabilities rose from ₹140 Cr at June to ₹289 Cr at September, a ₹149 Cr rise inside one quarter. [31]

web_blocks.title: Real-World Walkthrough 1: ₹100 Cr of market-entry sales, FY26 versus September 2026
paragraphs: The customer and the problem. A Make-in-India camera or components maker is too small to have credit lines from global suppliers. Its buyers (system integrators, corporates, government-linked EPCs) pay in 45 to 65 days. CNL steps between them: it sources the parts and finds the customer.

How the cash moves in FY26. CNL pays the vendor an advance, because the deck says vendor credit is limited, then ships, then waits about 70 days to be paid. Each ₹100 Cr of sales therefore ties up roughly ₹19 Cr of money (₹100 Cr × 70 ÷ 365). At a gross margin of about 3%, that sales line earns ₹3 Cr, and financing the ₹19 Cr at 10% costs ₹1.9 Cr, leaving ₹1.1 Cr before costs.

How it moves in September 2026. The same ₹100 Cr is now billed with customer advances in some cases and vendor invoices paid at about 66 days of purchases. On paper working capital is released and the balance sheet shows cash. Nothing about the underlying contract has changed except who is holding the float.

What it means. The margin on this business is a spread over cost of funds. Once suppliers or customers fund the float, ROCE jumps and operating cash flow swells; once they stop, both reverse. The earnings are real either way; the cash flow is only as stable as the float.

web_blocks.text: Sustainable or a timing reversal? The CFO answered directly on 29 October: 45 days ‘is not sustainable’ and normal is 52 to 55 days. [32] Our central case assumes 52 to 60 days on FY27 revenue 20% higher than FY26, and after-tax pre-working-capital cash of about ₹126 Cr. On that basis FY27 operating cash flow is ₹150 Cr to ₹220 Cr, with a negative H2 FY27 of ₹130 Cr to ₹205 Cr. If payables fall back to 45 days of purchases and customer advances to a third of September's level, about ₹290 Cr to ₹340 Cr flows back out. Net debt then returns to roughly ₹260 Cr to ₹310 Cr, close to March 2026's ₹302 Cr. So we estimate that 60% to 70% of the ₹479 Cr rise in payables and advances unwinds over three to four quarters. The CFO's own move from 45 to 52 to 55 days already concedes ₹60 Cr to ₹80 Cr of that. What persists is mostly a genuine BharatNet mobilisation advance, if that is what the advances are.

What a clean cash-conversion cycle looks like for this model. Brand sales need 90 to 120 days of capital by the CMD's own account. Market-entry sales need 55 to 65 days of customer credit plus advances to small vendors, and domestic receivables include 18% GST. [32][30] Our estimate of a clean cycle is 50 to 60 days of net working capital, which matches management's 52 to 55. On a ₹3,000 Cr annualised revenue run-rate that is ₹410 Cr to ₹490 Cr of working capital, against ₹337 Cr of trade working capital at September 2026. So ₹75 Cr to ₹150 Cr of the current position is borrowed from vendors and customers. Two definitions are in play. Management's net working capital days (42, 75 and 45 at March 2025, March 2026 and September 2026) match Screener's cash-conversion cycle at the two year-ends. Screener's separate working-capital days line reads 50 and 47 for the same years and is not used here. [29][33]

web_blocks.mechanism: A thin-margin intermediary reported large, steady profits for five years while cumulative operating cash flow was negative. It bridged the gap with bank and trade-finance lines until short-seller scrutiny, write-downs and a junk rating forced a debt-for-equity restructuring.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: From 2009 to 2014 reported net profit was S$2.4 billion against cumulative operating cash flow of −S$500 million and cumulative free cash flow of −S$2.4 billion (case-study figures). Over 2010 to 2014 turnover growth was +228% while inventory days fell from 26 to 13. In Feb 2015 it took a $440 million asset write-down, and in Dec 2015 it received a junk rating. It reported an annual loss of $4.9 billion in 2017. In Jan 2018 it agreed a $3.5 billion debt restructuring, with creditors taking 70% of the equity [41].
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: The tell was a multi-year gap between profit and operating cash flow that the headline growth hid. CNL's gap is different in kind. Its profits are margins on invoices that age cleanly (96.7% of receivables under six months) rather than fair-value gains. Even so, its cumulative FY19 to FY26 cash flow of −₹328 Cr against profit of ₹241 Cr has the same shape, so the H1 FY27 swing must be proven repeatable rather than assumed. [41][29][30]

web_blocks.title: Returns, interest cover and cumulative cash

web_blocks.caption: Working-capital ratios and ROCE, FY19 to FY26 (Screener ledger; days on year-end balances)
web_blocks.takeaway: Debtor days rose from 49 to 76, inventory days stayed at 24 to 25, and payable days slipped from 30 to 27. The cash conversion cycle went from 42 to 75 days and ROCE fell from 21% to 19% between FY25 and FY26. [29]

web_blocks.caption: Returns against an assumed cost of capital (consolidated; company figures from the Q2 FY27 deck; our computations from audited and reviewed statements)
rows: Our ROCE on average equity plus debt (pre-tax EBIT)
Our ROCE if the ₹282 Cr rise in payables were instead funded capital
Incremental ROCE FY25 to FY26: ΔEBIT ₹30.7 Cr ÷ Δcapital ₹330.5 Cr
Assumed cost of capital (equity 14.5%, debt 10% pre-tax, 14% tax, 55/45 weights)
web_blocks.takeaway: Average-capital ROCE of 18.7% beats a 12% cost of capital. The ₹330 Cr of capital added in FY26, however, earned only 8% after tax. The 19% H1 FY27 return falls to about 16% if the extra supplier credit is treated as funded capital. [33][30][31]

web_blocks.text: The computed statistics. Interest cover (EBIT ÷ interest) was 7.1x in FY25, 5.0x in FY26 and 3.8x in H1 FY27. Crisil prints 4.99x consolidated and 3.30x standalone for FY26, and its downgrade trigger is a sustained cover below 3x. [30][31][39] Cumulative operating cash flow for FY19 to FY26 was −₹328 Cr against cumulative profit of ₹241 Cr; cumulative free cash flow was −₹343 Cr. [29] Adding H1 FY27 gives cumulative operating cash flow of +₹23 Cr against profit of ₹281 Cr, and cumulative free cash flow of about +₹1 Cr. [29][31] The first half of FY27 therefore returned almost exactly what the preceding eight years consumed. Over the 18 months FY26 plus H1 FY27, operating cash flow of +₹79.4 Cr was 0.72x profit of ₹109.8 Cr and 0.47x EBITDA of ₹169.0 Cr. [30][31] That is the fairest single read of conversion.

web_blocks.text: Dilution is small. Shares outstanding were 1,50,16,675 at March 2026, unchanged during FY26 and up 6.4% from 1,41,13,675 at March 2024 after warrant conversions raised about ₹30 Cr in FY25. The preferential issue of 2023 was sized at ₹80.10 Cr in total. [37] The 2026 ESOP scheme allows up to 2,00,000 options (1.33%), and the Zicom SaaS share swap 2,25,000 shares (1.5%). Potential dilution is therefore about 2.8%. [30][42] Earnings per share of ₹41.04 is below profit per share of ₹46.8 because minority holders of Secure Connection take about 12% of group profit. [30] Dividend is ₹0.50 a share, about 1% of profit. [30][29]

web_blocks.caption: Probability-weighted judgement on earnings quality (our estimates for FY26 to FY28)
rows: Cumulative FY26 to FY28 operating cash flow at least 60% of profit because payables and advances prove structural
Profit is real; cash is consumed by growth at 50 to 60 days and funded by banks, TReDS and vendors at 9% to 11%; interest cover stays above 3x
The H1 FY27 inflow unwinds, interest cover falls toward 3x, or supplier-advance or receivable losses appear
web_blocks.takeaway: Profits are more likely than not real: we put the chance of a restatement or credit loss above 5% of profit at roughly one in seven. The chance that H1 FY27's cash flow represents durable cash-generating power is only about one in five. [30][31]

web_blocks.text: The single weakest assumption is that the ₹683 Cr of non-interest-bearing funding at 30 September 2026 is recurring working capital rather than quarter-end timing. That ₹683 Cr is ₹467 Cr of trade payables plus ₹216 Cr of other current liabilities, mostly advances. Everything favourable in H1 FY27, including 45 days, net cash and a 19% ROCE, depends on it. What would settle it: a quarterly balance sheet that splits other current liabilities into customer advances by project and shows the TReDS and buyers'-credit balance separately. We would also need payables ageing for the 30 September date and a monthly or average-balance disclosure of gross debt. The 31 December and 31 March balance sheets will answer most of it. A March 2027 balance sheet with net working capital at or below 55 days and cumulative cash flow still positive would move us from 20% to about 35% on genuine compounding.

book_paragraphs: Let me put two numbers side by side and ask you to sit with them. In the year to March 2026, Creative Newtech earned a profit of ₹70 Cr and its audited operating cash flow was minus ₹272 Cr. In the six months to September 2026 it earned ₹39 Cr and operating cash flow was plus ₹351 Cr. The first number says the business ate cash on a scale equal to four years of profit. The second says it produced almost nine times its profit in cash. Both come from signed financial statements, so neither is fiction. Our job is to work out which is the real company, or whether the truth sits between them. That is the whole of this chapter: not what the profit was, but where the money went and where it came from. If you remember only one thing, remember that a thin-margin intermediary can show you a spectacular cash number and a terrible one inside eighteen months without a single customer having changed.

Let me start with the P&L, because it is calmer. Imagine a ₹100 invoice. After paying the supplier you keep about ₹8.50 as gross margin in FY26, then spend about ₹4.70 on staff, freight, marketing and everything else, which leaves roughly ₹3.80 of EBITDA. Interest takes 76 paise, depreciation 6 paise, tax about 40 paise, and you are left with ₹2.59. Revenue has compounded at 33% a year for seven years, but notice how little of the growth is margin. EBITDA before other income was 2.8% of sales in FY19 and 3.4% in FY26. This is a volume business with a thin spread, and a thin spread is only safe if the money that finances each invoice is cheap and quick. That is what the cash-flow statement tests. One more detail, because it will come back: the tax rate was 14% on a consolidated basis and 25% on the standalone company, because the Hong Kong subsidiary that holds the Honeywell licence pays no tax. So the profit you are looking at is already tilted toward the entity that is hardest for an Indian investor to see into.

Now follow one March invoice through FY26. India sales jumped 165% to ₹1,797 Cr while sales outside India fell 18%, and domestic buyers pay in 60 to 65 days with GST on top. Receivables went from ₹238 Cr to ₹565 Cr, up 138% on 51% more sales. The CFO, Ajit Thakur, explained it on the 15 May 2026 call: ‘we are also getting into the new area of businesses like AI, surveillance and data center product line, where to get into the new area, we have to extend the extended credit.’ I find that honest and unpersuasive in equal measure. It is honest because credit is the price of entry. It is unpersuasive because the same executives had promised in May 2025 to bring working capital down to 35 days, and it went to 75. When a CFO's explanation and his predecessor's promise sit in two consecutive annual reports, I read the explanation as information and the promise as a lesson about how much weight to put on future ones.

Where did the money come from? From banks, and from a financing route you should know about. The CFO told the same call: ‘INR171 crores is the supply chain vendor financing for the MSME payment’, and the CMD added that the government platform lets small suppliers be paid within 45 days. That is TReDS, and it is classified as borrowing, not as trade credit. So the balance sheet showed debt rising from ₹72 Cr to ₹324 Cr, of which ₹171 Cr was really supplier credit that a bank had advanced early. I want you to remember this, because it makes the FY26 operating cash flow look worse than a pure trade-credit view would, and it will matter when we try to read the swing in H1 FY27. It also tells you something about a company's financing culture: when a vendor-finance platform is available at 8% to 9%, it is easier to keep growing than to chase a debtor, and no one in the room has a reason to stop.

Let me decompose FY26 properly. Of ₹435 Cr put into current assets, three-quarters went into receivables, 15% into inventory and 10% into advances to suppliers. If debtor days had stayed at last year's 49, operating cash flow would have been about minus ₹67 Cr, so roughly ₹205 Cr of the outflow was customers paying slower. Even then, the remainder is real: ₹66 Cr went into stock as memory and storage prices rose 30% to 40%, and ₹42 Cr into supplier advances. The company's own deck explains the second item: ‘vendor credit remains limited, resulting in higher advance payments.’ So here is the business in one sentence: it pays small suppliers early, sells to bigger customers late, and earns a spread of about 3% for carrying both ends. That is a perfectly respectable business, banks do something similar, but you would never value a bank without asking about its funding, and you should not read this company without asking the same question of its suppliers.

Now H1 FY27, and I want you to read the cash-flow statement the way a forensic accountant would, line by line. Operating profit before working capital was ₹63 Cr. Receivables took ₹52 Cr, supplier advances ₹116 Cr and inventory ₹13 Cr. Then trade payables added ₹282 Cr and other liabilities ₹193 Cr. After tax, the total is ₹351 Cr. Notice what that means: only ₹58 Cr of the ₹351 Cr is cash earned by the business after tax. The other 84% is liabilities growing faster than assets. Payables went from about 26 days of purchases to between 66 and 77 days. Nothing wrong with a supplier agreeing to wait, but you should ask how long a supplier is willing to be your bank. In a seasonal business the answer is usually until the season ends, and the season for this company's biggest quarter had not yet started when the half closed.

There is a small clue that I find more convincing than any commentary. In the September quarter the company paid ₹9.30 Cr of interest, the highest ever. At a blended cost of 9% to 11%, that is the interest on roughly ₹340 Cr to ₹410 Cr of debt, yet the borrowings on the balance sheet were only ₹194 Cr. The only way both are true is that the debt was high for most of the quarter and repaid at the very end. Cash tells the same story: ₹206 Cr in the bank on 30 September and ₹5 Cr six months earlier, when the same company was drawing on every bank line it had. When cash and payables both spike on one date, I treat the date as a photograph, not a film. Ask for the film: monthly balances. A company that told you its average debt through the quarter, not only its closing debt, would have answered this question in a single line, and one of the things I will ask for at the end of this chapter is exactly that disclosure.

Let me be fair about what could be genuine. Other current liabilities rose ₹197 Cr, and at March that line was 97% customer advances. The company won a ₹3,194.83 Cr BharatNet order in June with a consortium partner, and its own CFO described ordering ‘substantial material’ while waiting for quality certification from BSNL. Advance payments from a government-linked customer, matched by advance orders to suppliers, would show exactly this pattern: liabilities up ₹197 Cr, supplier advances up ₹112 Cr. That is a plausible and partly reassuring reading, but the filings do not say it. If it is right, those advances are not recurring cash flow either; they are mobilisation money that will be spent on equipment within a few quarters. I would put roughly even odds on that reading being the main explanation, which still leaves the other half of the jump in payables to be explained by supplier terms.

So is the inflow sustainable? The CFO told you himself on 29 October: ‘this is not sustainable to come to the level where we have to maintain this kind of level’, and normal is 52 to 55 days. I ran the arithmetic from there. At 52 to 60 days on revenue 20% higher, FY27 operating cash flow lands near ₹150 Cr to ₹220 Cr, which means H2 FY27 turns negative by ₹130 Cr to ₹205 Cr. If payables settle at 45 days of purchases and customer advances fall to a third, about ₹290 Cr to ₹340 Cr goes back out and net debt returns close to March's ₹302 Cr. My estimate is that 60% to 70% of the ₹479 Cr rise in payables and advances reverses over three or four quarters. Part of that is a concession management has already made, and the rest is a judgement you should hold loosely until the December and March balance sheets arrive.

What would a clean cycle look like? Think of the two businesses separately. Brands need 90 to 120 days of capital, by the CMD's own account, because you pay a factory and wait for Amazon, quick commerce or a Gulf distributor. Market entry needs 55 to 65 days of customer credit plus advances to small vendors, and your receivable includes 18% GST. Blend them and you arrive at 50 to 60 days of net working capital, which is management's own 52 to 55, and it is why I treat the year-end days as the number to track rather than the half-year days. On ₹3,000 Cr of annual sales that is ₹410 Cr to ₹490 Cr of working capital, against ₹337 Cr today. That gap of ₹75 Cr to ₹150 Cr is the part of today's position that belongs to your suppliers and customers, not to the company. Mind the labels: management's net working capital days match Screener's cash-conversion cycle at the year-ends, 42 and 75, while Screener's separate working-capital days line, 50 and 47, is a different formula that I do not use. If you ever need a rule of thumb, treat any working-capital improvement that cannot be traced to collections or to a shorter supply chain as a loan until proven otherwise.

Returns are where this shows up as a trap. The company reports ROCE of 21% for FY26 and about 28% annualised for FY27. My own calculation on average equity plus debt gives 18.7% for FY26, and the capital added in FY26 earned only 9.3% pre-tax, about 8% after tax, against a cost of capital near 12%. For H1 FY27 the 19% looks excellent until you notice that ROCE ignores payables. If the extra ₹282 Cr of supplier credit were funded capital, the return falls to about 16%. Add the cumulative picture and the lesson is sharper: eight years of cash flow summed to minus ₹343 Cr of free cash flow, and one half-year gave back ₹344 Cr. The company has spent a decade borrowing from its future and then, once, borrowing from its suppliers.

I will not leave you with only suspicion, because the evidence for the business is strong. The auditor gave unmodified opinions. Ninety-seven percent of receivables are under six months old, and the provision is ₹0.77 Cr. Crisil reaffirmed BBB+ in August 2026 and noted that the largest customer is now about 25% of revenue against 50% to 60% historically. The honest flags are narrower: about half of FY26 profit, ₹37 Cr of ₹70 Cr, is earned in Hong Kong subsidiaries audited by other auditors; the tax rate is 14% because that profit is untaxed; and one related-party balance, Click Retail at ₹47.74 Cr, is larger than its year's sales. Noble Group's profits were real, too, until the cash gap told a different story. I am not comparing the two businesses; I am comparing the shape of the numbers, and the lesson from Singapore is that the shape deserves an explanation before the story does.

So here is my judgement, with the probabilities attached. I put about 85% on the profit being economically real, and about 20% on genuine cash compounding, where payables and advances prove to be structural and cumulative cash flow tracks profit. I put 55% on the middle case, a real, cash-hungry growth business funded by banks and vendors at 9% to 11%, and 25% on stretch and reverse. The single weakest assumption is that ₹683 Cr of vendor payables and customer advances at 30 September is recurring. A quarterly balance sheet with the advances split by project, the TReDS balance shown separately and average debt disclosed would settle it. Until then, read the +₹351 Cr as a loan from the future, repayable in instalments. I would be delighted to be wrong, and the December quarter will tell us quickly.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The most important discipline in distribution analysis is to refuse a single-period cash number. Cash flow in this business is a seesaw: whoever holds the float gets the cash, and the float moves between customers, suppliers and banks more often than profit changes. Over eight years the seesaw ran one way; over six months it ran the other. The truth is in the average, and the average is still negative.

book_callouts.title: WHO HOLDS THE FLOAT?
book_callouts.text: For any thin-margin intermediary, ask three questions of every quarter-end balance sheet: how many days of the float are held by the customer, by the supplier and by the bank? Profit is the spread; cash flow is only a change in who holds the float. A good quarter is one in which the bank holds less, but only if the supplier did not simply hold more.
